question: Why do nurse researchers collect data in a study?

options.A: To replace traditional bedside shift reports completely
options.B: To prove that a chosen nursing theory is entirely wrong
options.C: To fulfill mandatory paperwork requirements for the hospital
options.D: To gather information needed to answer a research question

explanation: Think of data collection like gathering clues to solve a case. You collect specific info to answer your main research question! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h1)

question: Why is accurate data collection so important for evidence-based nursing?

options.A: It reduces the financial cost of purchasing hospital equipment
options.B: It eliminates the need for nurses to document patient vital signs
options.C: It ensures clinical decisions are based on solid proof rather than guesswork
options.D: It guarantees that every patient will recover without complications

explanation: Good evidence keeps our patients safe! Accurate data gives us the real facts we need instead of just guessing what works. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h1)

question: What makes data a 'primary source' in research?

options.A: Data retrieved from older textbooks found in the university library
options.B: Information published in international nursing journals last year
options.C: Patient records stored in the hospital archive from a decade ago
options.D: Information collected firsthand by the researcher for the current study

explanation: Primary data is fresh data you collect yourself right from the source for your own study! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h2)

question: A student nurse uses old patient admission files from last year to study malaria rates. What kind of data source is this?
explanation: Because someone else collected those files in the past, you are using a secondary source. It's like hand-me-down data! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h2)

question: Which of these is a biophysiological measure?
explanation: Biophysiological measures are physical or chemical checks on the body, like checking blood sugar or temperature. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h3)

question: What is the main feature of quantitative data collection?

options.A: They rely entirely on the researcher's personal feelings and intuition
options.B: They avoid using any structured tools or standardized checklists
options.C: They produce numerical data that can be measured and analyzed statistically
options.D: They focus exclusively on recording long, emotional personal stories

explanation: Quantitative data is all about quantities and numbers that you can run statistics on. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h3)

question: What is the main focus of qualitative data collection?

options.A: Counting the exact number of patient bed days in a month
options.B: Calculating hospital financial expenditures on medication
options.C: Understanding human experiences, emotions, and personal meanings
options.D: Measuring precise chemical levels in human blood samples

explanation: Qualitative data dives into quality, stories, and feelings rather than numbers. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h4)

question: Why do researchers use open-ended questions in interviews?

options.A: To make statistical data entry much faster for the computer software
options.B: To restrict the conversation to topics approved by the hospital board
options.C: To force participants to choose between 'yes' and 'no' answers quickly
options.D: To allow participants to describe their experiences fully in their own words

explanation: Open-ended questions let patients and participants tell their story freely without being boxed into a simple 'yes' or 'no'. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h4)

question: In research, what does 'reliability' mean?

options.A: Consistency of the data collection method or instrument
options.B: The total financial cost of purchasing the research equipment
options.C: How fast the researcher can finish interviewing participants
options.D: Whether the tool measures what it is supposed to measure

explanation: Reliability means consistency. If you use the tool again under the same conditions, you get the same steady results. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h5)

question: A researcher creates a survey for anxiety, but the questions actually measure physical hunger. What is wrong with this tool?
explanation: Validity is about whether your tool measures what it claims to measure. If it measures hunger instead of anxiety, its validity is off! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h5)

question: What does informed consent guarantee a research participant?

options.A: They will receive free lifetime medical care from the teaching hospital
options.B: Their names will be published on the front page of local newspapers
options.C: They are legally required to complete every single interview question
options.D: They understand the study and can withdraw at any time without penalty

explanation: Participation is totally voluntary! Patients must know what they are getting into and can walk away whenever they want. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h6)

question: What is the difference between anonymity and confidentiality?

options.A: Anonymity means no one can link data to a name; confidentiality keeps known identities secret
options.B: Anonymity is optional in nursing research; confidentiality is strictly mandatory
options.C: Anonymity applies only to secondary data; confidentiality applies to primary data
options.D: There is no difference between the two terms in clinical research studies

explanation: Anonymity means nobody (not even the researcher) knows whose data is whose. Confidentiality means you know who they are, but you keep their identity locked away safe. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h6)

question: Why do researchers run a pilot test before the main study starts?

options.A: To identify confusing questions and logistical flaws on a small scale
options.B: To force hospital administrators to approve the study immediately
options.C: To publish the final research paper ahead of all other researchers
options.D: To replace the need for formal ethical clearance from the review board

explanation: A pilot test is like a dress rehearsal. It helps you catch messy questions or flaws before you roll out the full study. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h7)

question: Why should a nurse researcher check completed questionnaires right after collecting them on the ward?

options.A: To destroy any forms that contain handwriting mistakes
options.B: To rewrite participant answers to fit the researcher's personal hypothesis
options.C: To catch and fix missing information while participants are still nearby
options.D: To grade the patient's literacy level based on their handwriting

explanation: Checking forms immediately lets you spot blank spaces and fix them while the participant is still right there! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h7)

question: Which of these is a secure way to store digital research data?

options.A: On a personal flash drive left unattended on a busy ward desk
options.B: As an unencrypted email attachment sent to personal social media
options.C: On password-protected institutional servers with regular backups
options.D: On an unsecured public website for anyone in the world to read

explanation: Always keep patient and research data safe using password protection and secure institutional servers. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h8)

question: What happens during 'data cleaning' after data collection?

options.A: Checking for entry mistakes, missing fields, and unusual outlier values
options.B: Translating all interview recordings into a different spoken language
options.C: Deleting any participant answers that do not support the hypothesis
options.D: Washing physical paper questionnaires with soap to remove hospital dust

explanation: Data cleaning means scanning your data for typos, blank spots, or weird errors before you start analyzing. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T15#GNS217_U3_T15_h8)
